metadata.title: Educational achievement among East Asian schoolchildren 1967–2020: A thematic review of the literature
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a thematic literature review and does not analyze microdata from PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS/FIMS or other ILSAs. Therefore, there is no student-level sampling frame, no plausible-value (PV) generation, and no application of complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight variance estimation. The included evidence is synthesized from 99 peer-reviewed studies (plus books/book chapters) rather than re-estimated from an ILSA dataset. As a result, weighting guidance for ILSA PV/scaling is not applicable to the review’s methodology; the review’s “sample” is the set of eligible publications identified through database searches and inclusion criteria.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this study does not estimate achievement scores from ILSA microdata (e.g., PISA/TIMSS PV-based domains). Instead, it synthesizes findings from previously published studies using a thematic coding approach. Missing-data handling is not reported because there is no original student-level dataset with item nonresponse or missing covariates to impute or delete; the unit of analysis is the included literature set.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study includes peer-reviewed journal articles, books, and book chapters published in English that focus on factors underlying educational achievement among East Asian schoolchildren (Grade 5–10) in Japan, China, South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore (with Hong Kong and Macau treated as urban regions of China). It excludes pre-school, upper-secondary, and higher education, and excludes conference papers, dissertations, and non-refereed books. The review uses database searches (ERIC, Google Scholar, PsycINFO, Web of Science) for 1967–2020 and applies thematic coding to included manuscripts; it does not define an analytic student sample from ILSA microdata.

The review reports that seven major themes with 53 sub-themes emerge, with cultural and educational-quantity factors dominating, followed by non-cognitive abilities, cognitive ability, educational quality (e.g., teacher competence), socioeconomic patterns, curriculum, and related system/process considerations. Because no PV-based achievement modeling is performed, there are no PV-handling, missing-data, or survey-weighting steps tied to ILSA scaling. data.outcome_summary: This article is a thematic literature review (not an empirical ML study) synthesizing 99 included studies published between 1967 and 2020 on educational achievement among East Asian schoolchildren (Grade 5–10) in Japan, China, South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore. It does not train or evaluate machine-learning models, and it does not re-estimate ILSA outcomes from microdata; instead, it codes included studies into themes and sub-themes using a qualitative content/thematic analysis approach. The review reports that seven major themes with 53 sub-themes emerge, with cultural and educational-quantity factors dominating, followed by non-cognitive abilities, cognitive ability, educational quality (e.g., teacher competence), socioeconomic patterns, curriculum, and related system/process considerations. Because no PV-based achievement modeling is performed, there are no PV-handling, missing-data, or survey-weighting steps tied to ILSA scaling. Limitations include potential incompleteness of the included literature and the subjectivity/categorical overlap inherent in thematic coding.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ILSA program/cycle, PV handling, missing-data strategy, ML algorithms, and numeric performance metrics because the paper is explicitly a thematic literature review rather than an empirical analysis of ILSA microdata. Consequently, there is no student-level dataset, no country-level analytic sample with n per economy, and no predictive modeling pipeline to extract. The “results” are thematic counts and narrative syntheses of prior studies, not model-based metrics.
